cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Let's start with a puzzle.
A wire carries current into a charging capacitor, but no charge crosses its
ideal vacuum gap.
How can the magnetic field around the circuit be consistent?
Maxwell's correction includes changing electric flux.
Displacement current is epsilon zero times the rate of change of electric flux
in vacuum.
It is not a stream of particles crossing the gap.
For ideal parallel plates, charge is epsilon zero times electric field times
plate area.
Differentiate: the displacement current across the full plate area equals the
charging current in the wire.
The magnetic circulation law includes conduction current plus displacement
current through the chosen surface.
Now give the plates circular radius a and assume uniform electric field,
negligible fringing and a quasistatic situation.
Take a circular magnetic loop of radius r less than a, concentric with the
plate axis, between the plates.
What fraction of electric flux does it enclose?
It is r squared divided by a squared.
So enclosed displacement current is charging current times that fraction.
Symmetry lets magnetic field magnitude be constant around the circular loop,
tangent to it.
Magnetic circulation is B times two pi r.
Equating it to mu zero times the enclosed displacement current gives B equal
to
mu zero I r divided by two pi a squared.
Notice the field increases linearly with r inside the plate area.
Try a equals zero point one metres, r equals zero point zero five metres and
charging current zero point two amperes.
Using mu zero divided by two pi approximately two times ten to the minus
seven,
the result is zero point two microtesla.
At the plate edge it is zero point four microtesla.
The current direction sets the circulation by the right hand rule.
This ideal capacitor model is not a universal field formula for arbitrary
leads, fringing or rapidly varying circuits.
Our key idea is to choose the surface carefully and include changing electric
flux where conduction current alone is not enough.
Now let the fields travel as a sinusoidal plane wave in vacuum.
Electric field, magnetic field and propagation direction are mutually
perpendicular.
Propagation follows electric field cross magnetic field.
Their peak magnitudes obey E zero equals c times B zero.
In vacuum, electric energy density is one half epsilon zero E squared.
Magnetic energy density is B squared divided by two mu zero.
Since B equals E divided by c and c squared equals one divided by mu zero
epsilon zero, those two densities are equal at each instant.
Total energy density is epsilon zero E squared.
The energy flux magnitude is c times that total density.
But intensity means the time average.
For a sinusoid, average E squared is half the peak amplitude squared.
Therefore intensity is one half epsilon zero c E zero squared.
If the field is given as RMS instead, intensity is epsilon zero c E RMS
squared, with no extra half.
Pause before substituting: is your number peak or RMS?
Let peak electric field be one hundred twenty volts per metre.
Use epsilon zero approximately eight point eight five times ten to the minus
twelve and c approximately three times ten to the eighth.
Peak magnetic field is zero point four microtesla.
Average intensity is nineteen point one one six watts per square metre, about
nineteen point one.
RMS electric field is one hundred twenty divided by the square root of two,
approximately eighty four point eight five volts per metre.
Putting that into the RMS formula gives the same intensity.
Double the amplitude and intensity becomes four times as large.
These relations assume a vacuum plane wave; do not automatically replace c
with
a medium speed while keeping every vacuum formula unchanged.
For the numerical answer, keep enough digits during calculation and round at
the end.
Finally, light can push.
At normal incidence, a completely absorbing surface receives momentum from the
incoming wave.
Average radiation pressure is intensity divided by c.
An ideal perfectly reflecting surface reverses the normal momentum, giving
twice that pressure.
These are normal incidence limiting cases, not formulas for every tilted or
partly reflecting surface.
Consider a beam with intensity six hundred watts per square metre striking
area
zero point zero two square metres normally.
Absorbed power is twelve watts.
Absorbing pressure is two times ten to the minus six pascals, and force is
four
times ten to the minus eight newtons.
For perfect reflection, force doubles to eight times ten to the minus eight
newtons.
A tiny force can still matter for light objects or sustained illumination.
Do not confuse force, measured in newtons, with pressure, measured in newtons
per square metre.
Now imagine an ideal source radiating one hundred twenty watts isotropically
into free space.
At distance two metres, power spreads over a sphere of area four pi r squared.
Intensity is one hundred twenty divided by sixteen pi, about two point three
nine watts per square metre.
At four metres it is one quarter as large, about zero point five nine seven.
Why?
Doubling radius makes the sphere's area four times larger while total emitted
power stays the same.
Plane wave local intensity formulas and spherical spreading describe different
aspects of the model; do not demand inverse square decay from an ideal
infinite
plane wave.
In this far field isotropic model, field amplitude scales as one over distance
because intensity scales with amplitude squared.
Real antennas, lasers, absorption and near fields can change the spatial
pattern.
The routine is to identify the wave model, decide whether the surface absorbs
or reflects, and distinguish total source power from the intensity arriving at
the surface.
